story_text.value:
Both me and my cofounder are in high school, and we're currently building Powermove, a video-editing tool that connects to an AI agent, letting users modify the app featureset, and generate effects and extensions.

We think this is the next step when it comes to software. We're already starting to see it, especially since a similar feature was just added recently in Claude Code. We believe that it will prove most useful in creative software though, and allow creatives to make essentially anything they want.

As a motion designer myself with a few years of experience, it has already turbocharged my outputs. The video you're seeing above was only possible with Powermove.

It's also completely free and open source.

story_text.value:
Every (personal) agent (like Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, Poke) asks you to connect your email, calendar, and tools again. Permissions are intransparent and every provider ends up building the same integrations.

We think there needs to be an independent tool that holds all connections to third party companies.

That way you can keep auth separate, audit what an agent does, set fine-grained permissions and easily switch between the agent apps.

I built this over the last few days with my friend Konsti. It's open source and we’ve put a lot of care into the self-hosting experience.

Now my Instinct has the same tools as Claude Code and Codex on my laptop.

What are your thoughts about this and how are you handling this today?

story_text.value:
The Enso Method is a new set of AI skills for Claude Code and Codex which I've open sourced on GitHub predominantly for developers who build for someone else who is making the product/business calls.

I've been using AI to write basically 100% of my code since late 2024, back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, when it barely worked and there were few people doing this and very little support for this way of developing. I stubbornly thought this was going to be the future and came up with a methodology for making it work, before "AI skills" were even a thing. Since then I've continued to refine the method and I just recently published it as open source. The method focuses on requirements (PRD, TDD) up front, and has skills that autonomously refine the requirements, declaring assumptions that should be validated by stakeholders. It doesn't expect you to be a solo founder or that whoever is at the keyboard directing Claude or Codex to be the product owner and business decider in addition to being the developer. I think most of us sit in the seat where we develop for someone else who decides. And if AI is all about velocity, then if we have to slow down to get product owners to review and decide, that puts a serious damper on the efficiency everyone expects from AI development. So a defining attribute of the Enso Method is, when it reviews the requirements prior to implementation, it asks what questions/gaps there are and it tries to answer its own questions. If it can get to 95%+ confidence in the answers, it just rolls with those. If less then it will declare the assumption in an assumptions.md file which gets routed to business stakeholders to review. In the meantime however we still consider this to be a green light, we can move forward and implement with the assumptions, and if we later hear from the business that the assumption was wrong, we update the requirements and re-implement, because implementation is now cheap, and waiting isn't.

title.value: Show HN: Enso Method – agent skills for building software for someone else

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 (https://agent37.com). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox.

You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo

We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses.

One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings.

Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month.

Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost:

* When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost.

* Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost.

* Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators.

* And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host.

We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques.

Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff.

I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya.

If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform.

Thanks!

https://agent37.com
